feed.title: Combined summary - Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols (DCPP): A Framework for Discussion

entry.title: Combined summary - Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols (DCPP): A Framework for Discussion
entry.summary: Recent advancements in the open-source mining ecosystem have catalyzed significant innovation in decentralized mining pool protocols, with notable initiatives such as Sv2, DATUM, and the [Open Mining Stack](https://www.256foundation.org/). These modern approaches are built on the foundations laid by earlier projects like P2Pool, which faced critical scaling challenges, particularly in managing coinbase-native payouts to a large miner base. The technical constraint of limited output slots per block, alongside Bitcoin’s scripting limitations and expanded attack surfaces, underscores the persistent complexity of designing robust Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols (DCPPs). As decentralized pools evolve, the ability to efficiently scale payout mechanisms remains central, necessitating solutions that balance fairness, security, and technical feasibility. The architecture of DCPPs must address three primary limitations: the scalability bottleneck of direct payouts due to output slot limits; an increased risk profile, as unreliable or uncompetitive payouts can render a pool economically unsustainable and vulnerable to targeted settlement griefing attacks; and the inherent restrictions of Bitcoin’s scripting language, which curtail the sophistication of protocol-level payout logic. In scenarios where more miners qualify for payment than available slots, pools often prioritize top contributors—a method prone to exploitation through identity splitting, known as the Rich List Attack (RLA). This strategy enables miners to divide their hashrate among multiple identities, thereby increasing their representation and marginalizing smaller participants, which introduces complex liabilities and necessitates advanced rules to safeguard equitable reward distribution. Several innovative schemes have been developed to counter these vulnerabilities. Chris Belcher’s 2017 [payment hub proposal](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=2135429.0) introduced off-chain payment channels managed by a central hub, employing multisig paths and timelocks to protect against stalling. Braidpool’s [Rolling Coinbase Aggregation (RCA)](https://github.com/braidpool/braidpool/blob/8d3c5198593d691f50ae5238cdaee215f4213cda/docs/braidpool_spec.mdpayout-update) accumulates rewards into a single UTXO, batching payouts using signatures from recent block-finding miners to economize on block space. P2Poolv2 envisions a [market-based model](https://github.com/p2poolv2/p2poolv2/wiki/Payout-mechanism---Trading-Shares-For-Bitcoin), enabling miners to swap sharechain UTXOs for Lightning payments via atomic swaps, aggregating sufficient value to secure coinbase slots. Each methodology, however, carries distinct risks—often shifting rather than neutralizing threats such as PSG. For example, Belcher’s model is susceptible to RLA if hubs are compelled to manage numerous low-value channels, while Braidpool’s RCA outputs present targets for accumulation by adversaries seeking signing authority. The P2Poolv2 system can also be manipulated by attackers distributing holdings across multiple identities. The ideal future for DCPPs would allow all participants to claim proportional, enforceable payouts without competing for ranked slots, eliminating incentives for identity splitting and unfair reward redistribution. Achieving this within Bitcoin’s current covenant and script limitations remains an ongoing challenge, compelling developers to pragmatically balance achievable technical advances with optimal fairness and security. Two principal tools emerge in this context: leveraging Bitcoin script and engaging external hashrate or liquidity markets. A promising direction involves coinpools funded directly from coinbase transactions, granting participants pre-signed exit transactions for unilateral withdrawal. Such systems require careful governance over threshold key holders and robust fallback mechanisms to ensure resilience against uncooperative actors. Case studies, such as integrating Spark or Ark structures within the P2Poolv2 framework, illustrate both opportunities and pitfalls. In a Spark-like model, professional service providers and elected market makers collectively control the coinbase output, allocating payout tree leaves to miners. However, this setup is vulnerable to the “poison pill” attack, where adversaries inflate subtrees with identities, transferring the majority and leaving minimal value, thus imposing costs on honest market makers. The adoption of standardized terminology—such as PSG and RLA—has brought much-needed clarity, enabling more precise discourse around these nuanced dynamics. Historical analysis of P2Pool operations provides valuable insight into payout distribution trends and technical thresholds. Data reveal that, during peak periods, a typical P2Pool block could distribute rewards to hundreds of addresses, peaking at 553 in a single transaction. The original code enforced a rule retaining only the 4,000 largest payouts, a limit never reached in practice. Small miners were primarily squeezed out by natural network growth and dust rules, which automatically increased share difficulty when expected payouts fell below 0.001 BTC. As a result, those unable to meet the threshold simply ceased receiving payments, not due to targeted attacks, but as an inevitable outcome of the protocol’s scaling constraints.
